content: The studies reviewed indicate that cold knife conization (CKC) may lead to higher risks of infection and bleeding compared to electrosurgical excision. Additionally, women who undergo CKC may have an increased likelihood of premature deliveries in subsequent pregnancies. Although the studies did not confirm the HIV status of participants, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) agreed that the findings could be extrapolated to women living with HIV and applied directly to this population. CKC is typically performed in an operating theater, which may limit its accessibility in certain settings. It is also more expensive and less preferred by women compared to large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ). The GDG emphasized the need for more data on the specificity and sensitivity of screening tests among women living with HIV, including those on antiretroviral therapy (ART). They also highlighted the importance of research on the prevalence of cervical pre-cancer and appropriate screening strategies for transgender men, non-binary individuals, and intersex individuals with a cervix. Special considerations and interventions are needed to overcome barriers to screening in these populations. Further research is required to determine whether there should be an upper age limit for self-sampling in cervical cancer screening. The GDG also noted the need to evaluate the optimal follow-up intervals after treatment, particularly for women living with HIV, who have a higher recurrence rate of HPV-related lesions. Longitudinal data on HPV recurrence and progression to invasive cancer in women living with HIV compared to the general population are also necessary. The GDG suggested initiating cervical cancer screening at age 25 for women living with HIV, including those with perinatally acquired HIV. They also called for more research on the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of CKC versus LLETZ in treating adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) in both the general population and women living with HIV. The integration of cervical cancer screening into HIV treatment programs was discussed, with a focus on whether this approach would increase screening uptake or risk being overlooked. Additionally, the GDG identified a need to understand why some women who screen positive are lost to follow-up and do not receive treatment. The dissemination of the final WHO guidelines will be carried out through WHO’s global network to ensure that healthcare providers and program managers have access to the latest evidence for preventing cervical cancer. The guidelines will be available for download on the WHO website and distributed in print upon request. They will also be shared at high-level meetings, international conferences, and through policy briefs tailored for women living with HIV and sexual and reproductive health programs. The guidelines will be translated into six official WHO languages, and regional workshops and webinars will be organized to support their adaptation and implementation at the national level. WHO will collaborate with regional and national partners, as well as other UN agencies, to ensure effective implementation and monitoring of the guidelines. The GDG plans to establish living recommendations for screening and treatment tests, which will be updated continuously as new evidence emerges. This process will include the evaluation of emerging technologies such as HPV mRNA detection, DNA methylation, p16/Ki-67 dual-staining cytology, and automated visual evaluation. These updates aim to provide the most effective and evidence-based strategies for cervical cancer prevention.
